discovery: Invention and development of the optical lattice atomic clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the optical lattice clock. The idea is to trap neutral atoms in a 'magic-wavelength' optical lattice, so that the trap does not perturb the clock transition. This combines the Doppler-free confinement of single-ion clocks with the high signal-to-noise of large atomic ensembles. Ye turned the concept into the world's most precise and accurate clocks. Using ultrastable lasers, degenerate Fermi gases and spectroscopy of many interacting atoms, his strontium clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and below. In 2022 these clocks resolved the gravitational redshift across a single millimetre-scale atomic sample. Lattice clocks have improved timekeeping by more than two orders of magnitude. They are driving the redefinition of the SI second, enabling relativistic geodesy, and setting new limits on variations of fundamental constants and on dark matter. This is a new measurement paradigm that unites fundamental physics and practical metrology.
